<reason>PRO won a well-fought, genuinely narrowed debate. Both sides executed the format cleanly (proper Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 structure) and the clash distilled to one question: does the motion add anything beyond existing platform password prompts? CON's best material — the fixed-bankroll argument (a $20 top-up is a claw machine with a coin pocket) and the cash-out distinction for casinos — was real pressure, and CON's pressure Q1 was sharp. But PRO answered it with the "dollar-blind PIN" point: the parent authenticates a currency pack, and the randomized pulls, hidden odds, and near-miss loops happen after the PIN, inside the game, which is exactly why odds disclosure, pull-counted caps, and cooling-off must live there. PRO also successfully harvested CON's own concessions: that minors are not load-bearing (emptying the motion's "even if" clause) and that the answer is "better defaults," which is the proposition itself. CON's proportionality case survived but never fully priced the asymmetric stakes PRO kept putting on the table (thirty-second toggle vs. bank statement). PRO made the debate easier to decide with a coherent synthesis ("every slot-machine feature, none of the kinder-egg constraints") and a closing that directly refuted CON's final image. Minor execution cost: two of PRO's turns were clipped, but little substance was lost. CON's "money comes back out" point about casinos went unanswered and keeps this from being a larger margin.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was CON's fixed-bankroll argument in the closing (a child cannot pull beyond the authenticated $20, so it is a claw machine with a coin pocket) met by PRO's "the parent authenticated a price, not a pull count" and the front-door-lock vs. slot-machine-in-the-bedroom reframe — which explained why the motion's in-game protections are not duplicative of platform settings and left CON's duplication objection without a clean answer.</best_rebuttal>
